planting.note: Move outdoors to a shaded, humid location once night temperatures stay above 55F; elsewhere grow year-round as a compact tabletop houseplant in bright, indirect light.

directions: This Thai-bred cultivar produces lance-shaped leaves splashed in pink, cream, and green in a pattern that holds up well even under the lower light levels typical of interior rooms, unlike some pink aglaonemas that revert to solid green under stress. Its compact, clumping habit rarely exceeds 16 inches, making it well suited to shelves, desks, and small tabletop containers. Let the top half of the potting mix dry between waterings, keep it out of direct sun which can scorch the pastel leaf tissue, and maintain warmth above 55F, since cold drafts quickly cause leaf spotting and decline.

planting.note: Move outdoors to a shaded location after temperatures remain reliably above 55F; in zone 9 place outdoors April-October and overwinter indoors, as with sibling cultivar Silver Bay.

directions: Diamond Bay arose as a somaclonal mutation of Silver Bay and was released by the University of Florida breeding program in 2002, distinguished by a central grey-green zone that covers just over half of each broad, lance-shaped leaf, bordered by irregular green margins. Its subdued, cool coloring reads as calmer and more understated than red- or white-patterned aglaonema cultivars, and it holds this pattern reliably across generations of production. Grow in low to bright indirect light in well-drained, humus-rich mix, let the surface dry slightly between waterings, and protect from temperatures below 55F and cold drafts.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension EDIS EP340

planting.note: Grow year-round as a compact indoor foliage plant in medium to bright indirect light; move to a shaded porch in summer once nights stay above 55F.

directions: Tigress carries lance-shaped leaves with bold, contrasting stripes of dark green and silvery white radiating outward from the midrib, a striped pattern more dramatic than the soft mottling of most other silver-toned aglaonema cultivars. It stays compact and clumping, rarely exceeding 18 inches, and is notably tolerant of low light and irregular watering, making it a forgiving choice for beginners. Allow the top two inches of potting mix to dry between waterings, keep it out of direct sun, and maintain temperatures above 55F to prevent chilling injury.

planting.note: Grow as a larger floor-height houseplant in medium to bright indirect light; move outdoors to a shaded patio only after nights stay reliably above 55F.

directions: Big Roy is among the larger-growing named aglaonema cultivars, with broad, rounded leaves marked in deep green, pink, and orange-red speckling that gives each leaf an individual, painterly variegation pattern. Its bigger stature and bolder pink coloring set it apart from smaller silver- or cream-patterned cultivars, making it a strong specimen plant for floor placement rather than a tabletop pot. Grow in medium to bright indirect light in well-drained potting mix, water when the top inch of soil dries, and avoid cold drafts and temperatures below 55F, which cause leaf chilling damage.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, fertile potting mix; Honeydew is frost-tender and grown outdoors only in zones 10-11.

directions: Honeydew produces large, broad leaves with vivid, near-solid golden-yellow centers edged in a contrasting green border, a brighter and warmer color scheme than the creamy-chartreuse tones of Camille or the deep green marbling of Tropic Snow. High humidity above 50 percent helps it hold its color and avoid crisping leaf edges indoors. Water when the top inch of soil dries, keep it away from cold drafts and direct hot sun, and prune back leggy canes in spring to promote fuller regrowth from the base; like all dieffenbachias, its sap is highly irritating if chewed and it should be kept from curious pets and children.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in medium to bright indirect light in well-drained, fertile potting mix; Panther is frost-tender and grown outdoors only in zones 10-11.

directions: Panther is a fast-growing, large-leaved dieffenbachia cultivar bearing deep green leaves up to two feet long, marked with irregular silvery streaks and light green speckling reminiscent of a big cat's dappled coat, a bolder and darker pattern than the pale-centered Camille or golden Honeydew. It tolerates lower light than many variegated dieffenbachias while still holding its speckled markings. Water when the top inch of soil feels dry, avoid overwatering since it is prone to root rot in soggy mix, and provide high humidity with occasional misting; the toxic sap makes it unsuitable for homes with plant-chewing pets or small children.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix; Sophia stays smaller and denser than Robusta, needing less floor space as it matures.

directions: Sophia is a solid-green rubber tree cultivar with smaller, rounder, glossier leaves and a denser, more compact growth habit than standard cultivars like Robusta, with a noticeable lime-green cast on the undersides of the leaves. Its tighter branching and reduced ultimate size make it easier to accommodate as an indoor floor plant in smaller rooms. Provide bright, indirect light, wipe dust from the leaves periodically to keep pores clear, water when the top inch of potting mix dries, and avoid moving it once situated, since rubber trees dislike sudden changes in light and location.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; site at a pond edge, stream bank, or bog garden where the soil never dries out during the growing season.

directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade with shelter from strong midday sun; never let the soil dry out. Primula pulverulenta is a tall Chinese candelabra primrose named for the conspicuous white mealy powder (farina) that coats its flower stalks and calyces, bearing several tiered whorls of deep wine-red to magenta-crimson flowers with a darker eye in early to midsummer, the strongest color among the widely grown candelabra species. The Bartley strain is a popular soft-pink-flowered selection sold alongside the typical crimson species. Like its relatives Primula bulleyana and Primula beesiana, it self-seeds readily in permanently damp ground and is best grown in drifts at a stream or pond margin in a woodland bog garden, zone 5-8.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; best sited at a pond edge, streamside, or damp low spot rather than an average garden bed.

directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade with protection from hot afternoon sun; never allow the soil to dry out. Primula beesiana is a Yunnan candelabra primrose closely related to Primula bulleyana, producing tiered whorls of rose-lilac to purplish-pink flowers with a small yellow eye on upright stems above coarse, tongue-shaped basal foliage in early summer. It hybridizes readily with other candelabra species where grown together, so plantings that include bulleyana, japonica, and pulverulenta nearby will often produce a colorful range of self-sown intermediates over time. A reliable, easy candelabra species for the damp margins of a woodland pond, stream, or bog garden, zone 5-8.

planting.note: Plant divisions in early spring in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade at a stream bank or bog margin; flowers emerge very early, often before the leaves fully expand, so mark the planting site to avoid disturbing the dormant crowns.

directions: Plant divisions in consistently wet, humus-rich soil at a stream bank, pond margin, or bog garden in partial shade; this diminutive Himalayan species is among the earliest primroses to bloom, sending up clusters of vivid rose-pink flowers directly from bare crowns in very early spring, with the crinkled bronze-green foliage expanding fully only after flowering. It is exceptionally cold hardy and thrives where its roots can sit in permanently saturated, humus-rich soil through the growing season, making it a natural companion for candelabra primroses, marsh marigold, and moisture-loving ferns at a pond or stream edge. Its small stature and brilliant, jewel-like color make it a striking early accent when massed in a damp rock garden pocket or bog bed, zone 3-8.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Julia's primrose spreads by creeping stems into a low mat and is easily divided every few years to make new plants.

directions: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to light sun; Julia's primrose is a low, mat-forming species from the Caucasus that spreads by short creeping stems to form a dense groundcover of small, rounded, glossy leaves studded with bright magenta-purple, yellow-eyed flowers in very early spring. It is the parent of the popular Juliana hybrid primroses, including the classic cultivar 'Wanda', and shares their extreme cold hardiness and tolerance of heavier garden soils than most primrose species. Its low, spreading habit makes it well suited to edging a shaded path, carpeting the base of shrubs, or filling gaps between stepping stones in a woodland garden, zone 4-8.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 12-14 weeks before setting out and transplant in cool weather into moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; fairy primrose is frost-tender and is usually grown as a cool-season bedding or container annual, or year-round as a houseplant.

directions: Start seed indoors in late summer and transplant into moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; fairy primrose is a Chinese species grown as a tender cool-season annual or winter-flowering houseplant, valued for its airy, well-spaced whorls of small, lightly fragrant flowers in white, pink, lavender, and magenta held on slender stems well above rounded, softly scalloped leaves. It blooms over a long cool-season period from late winter into spring and is a lighter, more delicate alternative to the coarser-leaved Primula obconica for shaded containers, window boxes, and porch displays in mild climates. Where winters are too cold for outdoor culture, grow it as a bright, cool indoor pot plant and treat it as a disposable annual after bloom.

planting.note: Plant offsets or container-grown divisions in early fall in gritty, humus-rich, sharply drained soil in partial shade; grow in pots under a cold frame or auricula theatre where the powdery farina on the leaves and flowers can be kept dry, since overhead rain and wet winters can spoil it and rot the crown.

directions: Grow in gritty, sharply drained, humus-rich compost in partial shade, ideally in a pot under cover where rain cannot spoil the flowers; keep evenly moist during active growth but never waterlogged. 'Old Irish Blue' is one of the oldest named auricula cultivars still in cultivation, a heritage 'self' type auricula prized by specialist growers for its clear violet-blue petals surrounding a neat, farina-dusted white paste eye, held above rosettes of thick, grey-green, mealy leaves. Like other show and border auriculas, it is traditionally grown in clay pots on tiered wooden auricula theatres or under glass, where its old-fashioned coloring and heavy farina can be displayed and protected at eye level. A collector's plant for auricula enthusiasts and a direct link to eighteenth-century florists' flower culture, best divided and repotted every one to two years after flowering.

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun on a slope or elevated site that drains cold air away from the bloom; Hargrand sets a much heavier crop with a compatible pollenizer such as Harcot or Harogem planted nearby, since fruit set from self-pollination alone is often light.

directions: Hargrand was released by the Harrow Research Station in Ontario, Canada, the same cold-hardy breeding program that produced Harcot and Harglow, and it is grown specifically for its exceptionally large fruit size relative to other hardy apricot selections. Skin is yellow-orange with a light red blush over firm, freestone flesh with good, well-balanced flavor for fresh eating and preserving. Because fruit set improves markedly with cross-pollination, plant Hargrand alongside another Harrow-series or mid-season apricot with overlapping bloom rather than relying on it as a stand-alone tree. As with other Harrow selections, winter cold is rarely the limiting factor; a planting site that avoids frost pockets during the early spring bloom period protects the crop far more than any additional winter protection.

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Harogem is self-fertile and needs no pollinizer, and typically ripens a few days ahead of Harcot.

directions: Like its better-known sibling Harcot, Harogem came out of Agriculture Canada's Harrow Research Station breeding program in Ontario aimed at combining northeastern cold hardiness with better disease resistance than California apricots typically offer. Fruit is medium-sized with orange skin blushed red and firm, flavorful flesh, ripening in a tight window just before Harcot in most seasons. The tree is self-fertile, so a single planting will bear fruit, and it carries useful tolerance to perennial canker and brown rot, diseases that are a persistent problem for apricots in humid eastern climates. Thin fruit after natural June drop and prune to an open center for good airflow, which further reduces disease pressure in wetter regions.

common_name: Perfection Apricot (Large-Fruited California Heirloom Requiring a Pollenizer)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Perfection is self-unfruitful and must be planted near a compatible pollenizer such as Blenheim or another early-blooming apricot to set a crop.

directions: Perfection is an early-twentieth-century California apricot bred for exceptionally large fruit size, among the biggest of the traditional apricot varieties, with golden-orange skin and juicy, mild-flavored flesh best suited to fresh eating rather than drying. Unlike self-fertile modern varieties, Perfection will not set a reliable crop on its own and needs a compatible pollenizer, typically Blenheim, planted within pollinating distance and blooming at the same time. The tree tends to set fruit heavily in good years, so thin aggressively while fruit is still small to prevent limb breakage and to keep the remaining fruit at full large size. Because it is an older variety selected before modern disease-resistance breeding, watch for brown rot and bacterial canker in humid conditions and prune for an open canopy to improve air circulation.

common_name: Wenatchee Moorpark Apricot (Pacific Northwest Large-Fruited Self-Fruitful Apricot)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; self-fruitful, so a single tree will bear, though a nearby pollenizer can improve fruit set in cool maritime springs.

directions: Wenatchee Moorpark takes its name from Washington's Wenatchee Valley fruit-growing district, where it was selected as a more reliably productive, self-fruitful alternative to the old English Moorpark type it resembles in fruit quality. Fruit is large with golden-orange skin and a red blush, and richly flavored flesh good for fresh eating, canning, and drying. It has become a favorite home-orchard apricot in the Pacific Northwest because its moderate chill requirement suits the region's maritime winters while its bloom holds up reasonably well against the area's variable, wet springs. As with most apricots grown in the Northwest, watch for brown rot in wet spring weather and prune to an open form for good air circulation through the canopy.

common_name: Kudos Ambrosia Agastache (Compact Creamy-Peach Hummingbird Mint)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; sharp drainage is essential for winter survival since agastache crowns rot readily in wet, heavy soil.

directions: Kudos Ambrosia forms a tight, mounding clump of aromatic gray-green foliage topped with soft plumes that blend creamy coconut, pale peach, and light rose-pink tones in the same spike, giving it a distinctive multi-hued look among hummingbird mints. Bloom runs from early summer into fall and draws bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds steadily. Its compact, self-supporting habit needs no staking or deadheading to keep flowering. Provide lean, sharply drained soil and full sun, and keep it dry over winter to protect the crown from rot.
sources: Terra Nova Nurseries plant introduction notes

common_name: Kudos Gold Agastache (Compact Lemon-Gold Hummingbird Mint)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; sharp drainage is essential for winter survival since agastache crowns rot readily in wet, heavy soil.

directions: A wider-spreading, lower-growing member of the Kudos series, Kudos Gold produces dense spikes of clear lemon-gold flowers over aromatic, anise-scented foliage from early summer through fall. Its broad, mounding habit fills out garden edges and container plantings without becoming leggy. The long, continuous bloom period keeps bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds coming back throughout the season. Give it lean, well-drained soil in full sun and avoid winter wet to help the crown overwinter reliably.
sources: Terra Nova Nurseries plant introduction notes

common_name: Kudos Red Agastache (Compact Scarlet Hummingbird Mint)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; sharp drainage is essential for winter survival since agastache crowns rot readily in wet, heavy soil.

directions: The lowest, widest-spreading selection in the Kudos series, Kudos Red hugs the ground in a broad mat of aromatic foliage while sending up short, dense spikes of vivid scarlet-red flowers from early summer into fall. Its ground-covering habit suits rock gardens, hot dry slopes, and the front of a sunny border. The intense flower color is a strong hummingbird draw throughout the bloom season. Plant in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun and keep it on the dry side over winter to protect the crown.
sources: Terra Nova Nurseries plant introduction notes

common_name: Kudos Silver Blue Agastache (Compact Soft-Blue Hummingbird Mint)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; sharp drainage is essential for winter survival since agastache crowns rot readily in wet, heavy soil.

directions: Kudos Silver Blue pairs soft, clear light-blue flower spikes with silvery-green, anise-scented foliage, giving it a cooler-toned presence than most hummingbird mints. The broad, mounding habit blooms continuously from early summer through fall, drawing bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds. It combines especially well with warm-colored perennials thanks to its muted, silvery-blue palette. Grow in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun, and keep the crown dry over winter to prevent rot.
sources: Terra Nova Nurseries plant introduction notes

common_name: Poquito Dark Blue Agastache (Dwarf Compact Hummingbird Mint)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; sharp drainage is essential for winter survival since agastache crowns rot readily in wet, heavy soil.

directions: One of the most diminutive hummingbird mints available, Poquito Dark Blue packs dense spikes of deep violet-blue tubular flowers onto a tight, bushy plant barely 10 inches tall, making it ideal for containers, rock gardens, and the front edge of a sunny border. Fragrant, fine-textured foliage backs a long bloom season from late spring through fall. It is heat- and drought-tolerant once established and draws hummingbirds and bees reliably. Give it lean, sharply drained soil and full sun, and avoid winter wet to help the crown overwinter successfully.
sources: Terra Nova Nurseries plant introduction notes

common_name: Poquito Lavender Agastache (Dwarf Compact Hummingbird Mint)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; sharp drainage is essential for winter survival since agastache crowns rot readily in wet, heavy soil.

directions: Poquito Lavender forms a tidy, bushy mound scarcely a foot tall, covered in soft lavender-purple flower spikes from late spring through fall. Its diminutive size makes it a natural fit for containers, small borders, and sidewalk strips where taller agastache would overwhelm the space. Aromatic, anise-scented foliage and steady bloom draw bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds all season. Plant in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun, and keep the crown dry over winter to prevent rot.
sources: Terra Nova Nurseries plant introduction notes

common_name: Apache Sunset Hummingbird Mint (Compact Sunset Hyssop)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost or set out nursery plants after frost danger passes, into very well-drained, lean, alkaline soil in full sun; excellent drainage is critical, as rich or wet soils promote crown rot and weak, floppy growth.

directions: A more compact selection of the species than the wild form, Apache Sunset stays a tidy 18 to 20 inches tall while producing the same intensely fragrant, licorice-and-root-beer-scented gray-green foliage and long, narrow spikes of salmon-orange flowers that shade to pink at the tips. Bloom runs from midsummer through fall and is a magnet for hummingbirds, with bees and butterflies visiting steadily as well. It thrives in hot, dry, alkaline soils typical of the Southwest and is notably heat- and drought-tolerant once established, though like the species it is short-lived and benefits from being allowed to self-sow. Deer and rabbit resistant.
